label: explain-leanbio-enhancers
one_line: We test whether a DNA switch's strength depends on which gene it drives, and how to tell that from chance.
what: Cells have DNA switches called enhancers. Each one turns up a gene through a second switch called a promoter. We ask a simple question. If you rank enhancers from weakest to strongest on one promoter, does the order stay the same on another promoter? If it does, each enhancer just has one strength. If it does not, strength depends on the pairing. We reread a public data set of 98 enhancers on 15 promoters. We also ran a computer simulation of pure chance, and we wrote a computer-checked proof of what simple models allow.
why: Doctors and engineers want to design DNA switches that work in a chosen gene. That is easier if an enhancer has one fixed strength. It is harder if strength depends on the partner. Studies so far disagree, so a clear test helps. We do not claim a final answer here. We claim only a sharper way to ask.

steps.text: We read the main papers on this question. A large human study found a simple multiplying pattern. Fruit fly and mouse studies found more picky pairings.
steps.picture: Reading three reviews of the same restaurant before you eat there.

steps.text: We took a public data set from mouse cells. It has 98 enhancers, each measured on 15 promoters, with 3 repeats of every measurement.
steps.picture: Timing 98 runners on 15 different tracks, three times each.

steps.text: For each pair of promoters we asked how well the enhancer ranking agrees. A score of 1 means the same order. A score of 0 means no link.
steps.picture: Comparing two teachers' grade lists for the same class.

steps.text: We counted clear-cut pairs of enhancers whose order flips between promoters. We compared that count with what measurement noise alone would give.
steps.picture: Checking if a coin that landed heads 60 times is really unfair.

steps.text: We fitted the simplest pattern, where each enhancer has one strength that every promoter multiplies. Then we measured how much was left over.
steps.picture: Fitting a straight ruler to a curved line and measuring the gap.

steps.text: We ran a computer simulation with no real pairing effect at all. It shows how often noise alone swaps the order of enhancers.
steps.picture: Shuffling a deck many times to see what luck looks like.

steps.text: We wrote a proof, checked by a computer, about simple models. It shows a ceiling on strength can make two enhancers tie but never swap.
steps.picture: Proving that a speed limit can make two cars tie but never makes the slower one win.

steps.text: We also proved what a flip does not tell you. Several different causes could give the same flip.
steps.picture: A wet street can mean rain, a hose or a passing truck.

steps.text: We suggest one extra experiment. Turn each enhancer up in steps on two very different promoters, and repeat every measurement three times.
steps.picture: Turning a volume knob in steps on two different speakers.

wrong_if: Our bet, written down before looking, is this. In real data, enhancer order flips between promoters more often than noise alone predicts. If flips were no more common than that chance baseline, we are wrong. Then one fixed strength per enhancer would be enough.
could_go_wrong: The 98 enhancers are DNA stretches that look like switches, and nobody tested each one on its own.
We had only 3 repeats per measurement, so our estimate of noise is rough.
Our chance simulation assumes tidy, even noise, but real counts are messier, especially for weak enhancers.
We could not read the large human data set, so we did not rerun that analysis ourselves.
Two of the sources are early drafts that other scientists have not yet reviewed, and we read only their summaries.
The extra experiment we suggest is a prediction from a simulation, not a result from a lab.
We have not compared the real flip counts with the chance baseline built in our own simulation, so that final step is still undone.
Studies disagree, and their different designs may explain some of the gap.

questions.a: We reran public data and got the numbers in the check list below. A second set of checkers confirmed most of the key claims. Some were only partly confirmed, and we say so.

We did not rerun the large human data set. We did not test each enhancer in a lab. We did not compare real flip counts with our own chance simulation. We do not know how big the effect is in most human cells.

questions.q: Is the answer yes or no?
questions.a: We do not know. The mouse data show real pairing effects. The big human study found a mostly simple pattern. Both can be partly true.

questions.q: How big is the pairing effect in the mouse data?
questions.a: A simple one-strength pattern explains about 71 percent of the variation. The leftover pairing effect is about 12 times bigger than measurement noise.

questions.q: Can noise alone fake a flip?
questions.a: Yes. With no real pairing at all, 1.3 to 43.7 percent of enhancer pairs change order. So a raw count of flips proves little.
It rules out the simple models we proved things about. It does not say which cause is true. Several different causes give the same flip.

questions.q: Why does a ceiling on strength matter?
questions.a: Strong enhancers can all hit the same top level. Our proof shows that a ceiling can make them tie but not swap places.
Test each enhancer at several strengths on two very different promoters, with three repeats. That separates a ceiling from a true mismatch.

A result that depends on which enhancer is paired with which promoter.

A computer program that checks each step of a maths proof.

left_out: Claim that the proof file passes the project check with no errors: the verifier could not re-run it (not checkable), so we cite only the file and its fingerprint.
The wording '26% of clear-cut orderings reverse overall': the overall share is 29.0% (65,174 of 224,658); 26% is the typical per-pair share, so we use 'about a quarter' only for the typical pair.
The claim that the 98 by 15 panel is stated by the public data source: it is our own chosen subset, so we describe it as ours.
The claim that published data leave a ceiling versus a true mismatch open: only partly supported and mostly our inference, so we phrase it as 'we do not know'.
The claim that weak promoters are boosted most and that this can reorder enhancers: only partly supported and partly inference, so we do not state it as fact.
Any [held-out clade]-related source: excluded by the holdout rule.
